title: MCI: Bus vs Tanker, 34 Casualties (Triage Scenario)
chiefComplaint: Mass casualty incident, first wave arriving in 6 minutes
diagnoses: Mass casualty incident with capacity failure
Inhalational injury from the tanker fire
background: A tour bus and a fuel tanker collided on the elevated expressway at 21:40. Thirty-four casualties reported, at least eight critical, with a fire at scene. Your department has 4 resuscitation bays, 18 monitored cubicles, two general surgeons on call, one operating theatre available and 6 units of O negative blood in the fridge. Two other hospitals are receiving casualties. You are the most senior emergency physician in the building and the trauma consultant is 30 minutes away. The vital signs shown belong to the index patient described below, who is the first casualty through the door and the first triage decision you will be judged on.

exam.finding: Index patient: 34 year old male, thrown from the bus, cold and grey, GCS 9, obvious deformity of the left thigh. He walked past triage on a stretcher into resus one, and the question is whether he should have

Facial soot and singed nasal hairs from the tanker fire, hoarse voice, no stridor yet. Nine of the thirty-four casualties have similar airway findings and there are four ventilators available in the whole hospital

Tachycardic at 148/min, systolic 76, radial pulse impalpable and femoral pulse weak. Under the START triage system an impalpable radial pulse with a respiratory rate above 30 places him in the immediate (red) category

Reduced air entry on the left with hyperresonance and tracheal shift, consistent with a tension pneumothorax. This is treatable in 60 seconds at the door and is the classic thing that gets missed when everyone is counting casualties
Distended and rigid. Positive eFAST with free fluid in Morison's pouch and the pelvis. He needs the one available operating theatre, and three other red patients also need it
Cold and mottled, partial thickness burns to about 12% of the body surface over the right arm and flank, open left femoral fracture with ongoing bleeding controlled by a tourniquet applied at scene

GCS 9 (E2V3M4), moving all limbs, pupils equal. In a mass casualty setting, a GCS that is low from shock rather than from head injury is a resource question and not a neurological one, because it will improve with blood

investigations.name: Departmental capacity audit
investigations.value: 4 resus bays / 18 cubicles / 1 theatre / 6 units O negative / 4 ventilators
investigations.report: Thirty-four casualties against these numbers. In a mass casualty incident the limiting reagent is never knowledge, it is theatre time, blood and ventilators, and the plan must be written against those three numbers rather than against the number of patients.

investigations.name: START triage distribution at 40 minutes
investigations.report: Eight immediate patients against four resuscitation bays and one theatre. Retriage every patient every 15 minutes, since yellow patients become red and green patients walk out and collapse in the car park.

investigations.name: eFAST (index patient)
investigations.report: Free fluid in Morison's pouch and the pelvis. Absent lung sliding on the left with a lung point. Confirms both a haemoperitoneum and a left pneumothorax. In a mass casualty incident eFAST is the triage tool that decides who gets the theatre, because it takes 90 seconds and CT does not.

investigations.name: Blood bank status
investigations.value: 6 units O negative on site, 20 more units 45 minutes away
investigations.report: Six units against eight red patients. Activating the regional blood transport at the first call rather than after the fourth unit is used is the difference between having blood at minute 45 and at minute 90.

investigations.name: Blood gas and lactate (index patient)
investigations.report: Severe shock with a significant carboxyhaemoglobin level from the fire. Base deficit is the best available triage discriminator for who needs blood and theatre first.

investigations.name: Portable chest and pelvis X-ray
investigations.report: Left pneumothorax now decompressed with a chest drain in situ. No widened mediastinum. Pelvis intact. Left femoral shaft fracture. Portable films only. Nobody goes to the CT scanner during the first wave, because the scanner corridor becomes a queue and the queue becomes the bottleneck.

data.label: Declare the incident and take a role rather than a patient
actions: Declare a major incident and activate the hospital plan
Appoint yourself or a named colleague as medical commander
Appoint a separate triage officer at the door
Clear the department: discharge or move every patient who can be moved

doseMap.Appoint yourself or a named colleague as: The commander does not treat patients. The commonest failure in a mass casualty incident is that the most experienced clinician takes the first critical patient and the department loses its only person with the whole picture

data.label: Triage at the door with a fixed system, and do the 60 second interventions only
actions: START or equivalent triage at the entrance
Open the airway and decompress a tension pneumothorax, nothing more
Apply tourniquets to catastrophic haemorrhage
Tag every patient and record the time

doseMap.Open the airway and decompress a tension: At triage you are allowed only interventions that take under a minute and save a life. Starting a full resuscitation at the triage point stops triage, and the queue behind you loses more people than you save

data.label: Allocate the scarce resources explicitly, and write the allocation down
actions: Assign the operating theatre by expected survival benefit
Assign the 6 units of O negative
Assign the 4 ventilators
Activate regional blood transport and mutual aid immediately

doseMap.Assign the operating theatre by expected: The greatest good for the greatest number, which means the patient who needs the least theatre time to survive goes first, not the sickest. This is the ethical inversion of everyday practice and it must be a stated decision with a name against it

data.label: Index patient stabilised, and he is not first to theatre
data.narrative: Left chest drain at the door improves saturations to 94% and systolic to 92 with 2 units of blood. eFAST is positive but he is a responder. A second red patient with an unresponsive positive FAST and a systolic of 60 takes the theatre first. Your patient goes second, 35 minutes later. Both survive. Had you taken the theatre for the patient in front of you, the other would not have.

data.label: Assign someone to the expectant patients rather than leaving them in a corridor (Empathy)
data.narrative: Two patients are triaged expectant: unsurvivable injuries with the resources available tonight. The efficient thing is to move them to a side room and forget them. You assign a nurse and a chaplain, write analgesia and sedation orders for both, and say out loud to the team that expectant does not mean abandoned. One of them is conscious for eleven minutes and has someone holding her hand for all of it. Pi Pim says afterwards that this is the part of major incident training nobody drills and the part everyone remembers for the rest of their career.

data.label: Retriage every 15 minutes and control the second wave
actions: Formal retriage of all yellow and green patients every 15 minutes
Designate a separate area for walking wounded away from the resuscitation area
Assign a scribe to maintain a single casualty board
Refuse further ambulances once capacity is reached

doseMap.Refuse further ambulances once capacity: Diverting to the two other receiving hospitals is a clinical decision, not an administrative one. Accepting patients you cannot treat converts one overwhelmed department into two

data.label: Damage control surgery and staged definitive care
actions: Damage control laparotomy rather than definitive repair
Pack, close and return to ICU
Stage all orthopaedic fixation
Reassess burns and inhalational injuries as the second priority wave

doseMap.Damage control laparotomy rather than de: Forty minutes per patient instead of three hours. With one theatre and eight red patients, operative discipline is a triage tool

data.label: Six hour outcome
data.narrative: Thirty-four casualties received across three hospitals, of whom your department took 19. Two died at scene, two were triaged expectant and died within the hour, one died in theatre. Fourteen survived to ICU or ward admission. The index patient survives with a splenectomy, a femoral nail on day 3 and a resolved inhalational injury.

data.label: Debrief the department before anyone goes home
actions: Structured hot debrief within 2 hours
Identify the specific system failures, not the individuals
Arrange psychological support for staff and for the expectant patients' families
Formal review within 2 weeks

doseMap.Structured hot debrief within 2 hours: The junior staff who tagged the expectant patients need this more than the consultants do, and they are the ones most likely to be sent home first

data.label: Disposition
data.narrative: The debrief identifies three fixable failures: blood transport was activated at minute 22 rather than minute 2, there was no pre-designated walking wounded area, and nobody owned the casualty board for the first 18 minutes. All three are changed within a month. The department performs measurably better at the next incident, which is the only useful definition of a good outcome from a night like this.
